title: My Beloved Child
subtitle: 2 Timothy 1:1–2
description: Paul, an apostle by the will of God according to the promise of life, greets Timothy, his beloved child, with grace, mercy, and peace.
paragraphs: The second letter to Timothy opens in two verses, and nearly everything about it is different in temperature from the first. Paul names himself the way he always does at the head of a letter to his young coworker, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God. But where the first letter grounded his apostleship in a command, this one grounds it in a promise: he writes “according to the promise of life in Christ Jesus.” The authority and the hope arrive in the same breath. He is an apostle because God willed it, and the errand itself is life, promised and kept in Christ.

Then comes the address, and the whole letter's tone is inside it. The first letter called Timothy his true child in the faith, the son whose belonging Paul had certified to a church that might question him. This letter needs to certify nothing. Paul writes “To Timothy, my beloved child.” The Greek family word sits there without defense or explanation, and readers meeting the letter for the first time should let it land before anything else does: whatever follows, instructions, warnings, farewells, it is written inside a love that does not have to argue for itself.

The blessing follows the shape of the first letter's greeting, and it is worth hearing whole: “Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.” Two letters to the same man, and both open with mercy folded into the greeting where Paul's letters to churches usually carry grace and peace alone. Mercy is the word for help needed by a man in trouble, and by the end of this short opening a reader knows the essentials: an apostle speaking by God's will and God's promise, a beloved child receiving, and a blessing with mercy in it, sent from the Father and from Christ Jesus our Lord.

What the greeting does not say is part of its weight. It does not say where Paul is, though the verses ahead will call him a prisoner and speak of his chains. It does not say that this is the last letter of his we have, though everything in it leans that way. It simply opens the door: a father in the faith writing to his beloved child, under a promise of life. The next words turn to memory, to Timothy's tears, and to a grandmother and mother in whom faith lived first.

title: The Faith of Lois and Eunice
subtitle: 2 Timothy 1:3–5
description: Thanksgiving night and day, the remembered tears of a parting, and the sincere faith that dwelt first in Timothy's grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice.
paragraphs: The greeting barely closes before the letter turns to prayer and memory. Paul gives thanks for Timothy, and the thanksgiving carries his own history inside it: “I thank God, whom I serve with a clear conscience as did my forefathers, as I constantly remember you night and day in my prayers.” The God he thanks is the God of his ancestors, served across generations before him, and the man writing is not young in the faith or new to gratitude. Night and day, in prison, the young coworker is remembered. Thanksgiving here is not a formality at the top of a letter. It is the first thing a chained apostle does with his oldest partnership.

What he remembers most, he says next, is a parting: “Recalling your tears, I long to see you so that I may be filled with joy.” The letter does not say when the tears fell or where the two men last stood together. It keeps only the tears themselves, remembered by the man who saw them, and the longing they left behind. Paul, who in the first letter commanded and corrected like a supervisor of the work, writes here like a man who misses his friend. The joy he expects has a face and a meeting attached: seeing Timothy again would fill it.

Then the memory goes one generation further back than Timothy himself. “I am reminded of your sincere faith, which first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice, and I am convinced is in you as well.” These are the only verses in the New Testament that name Timothy's mother and grandmother. Acts had told readers that his mother was a Jewish believer and left her nameless. This letter, near the end of Paul's road, writes the names down: Lois first, then Eunice, then Timothy. The faith traveled the household in order, grandmother to mother to son, and Paul uses a household word for it. It dwelt in them, lived at home in them, and he is convinced, not merely hopeful, that it dwells in Timothy too.

Notice what kind of faith it is: sincere, the unhypocritical kind, faith without a mask on it. And notice what Paul does with the memory. He does not use the women as decoration around Timothy's story. He treats them as the faith's first addresses, the places it lived before it lived in the man he is writing to. A young minister wondering whether his own faith is really his, or only inherited scenery, is being told something exact: the same faith that dwelt in Lois and in Eunice dwells in him as well, and the apostle who knows him best is the one convinced of it. The next words take that inheritance and tell him to stir what he has been given into flame.

title: Fan into Flame
subtitle: 2 Timothy 1:6–12
description: Fan into flame the gift given through Paul's hands; the spirit not of fear but of power, love, and self-control; suffering joined for the gospel; and I know whom I have believed.
paragraphs: From the inherited faith, Paul turns to the gift Timothy received in person. “For this reason I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands.” A gift can bank down like coals under ash, still real, still hot at the core, and yet needing to be stirred before it blazes. Paul does not tell Timothy to go find a gift he lacks. He tells him to fan the one already in him, given when Paul's hands were laid on him, the commissioning the church at Lystra and the elders knew. The fire's tending is Timothy's work. The fire itself is God's.

Then the letter states one of its most carried sentences, and it should be heard at full strength: “For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.” Timothy's situation held real reasons for shrinking back, a teacher opposed, an apostle in chains, a church wobbling. Paul does not argue with the danger. He names what God gave instead of fear, and the three gifts answer the moment in order: power for the work, love for the people, self-control for the man himself. Whatever trembling Timothy knew, Paul refuses to let him call it God's gift.

The charge that follows joins suffering to the calling rather than excusing Timothy from it: “So do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, or of me, His prisoner. Instead, join me in suffering for the gospel by the power of God.” Ashamed is the danger word, not pain. Paul expects the gospel to cost his child something, and he asks him to pay it in company, by God's power and not by grit. Then the sentence opens into the gospel itself: “He has saved us and called us to a holy calling, not because of our works, but by His own purpose and by the grace He granted us in Christ Jesus before time began.” Before there was a Timothy to tremble or a Paul to chain, the grace was already granted. “And now He has revealed this grace through the appearing of our Savior, Christ Jesus, who has abolished death and illuminated the way to life and immortality through the gospel,” the errand “to which I was appointed as a preacher, an apostle, and a teacher.”

It is because of that errand that the chains exist, and Paul says so without flinching: “For this reason, even though I suffer as I do, I am not ashamed; for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that He is able to guard what I have entrusted to Him for that day.” Earlier tellings of Paul's charges had Timothy guarding what God entrusted to him. Here the direction reverses, and both stand: the apostle near the end of his road has placed his own deposit with God and is convinced God can keep it until that day, the day this letter keeps glancing toward. The confidence is not in the strength of his grip. It is in the one he has believed. From the man's own security, the letter turns back to Timothy's guard duty.

title: Guard the Treasure
subtitle: 2 Timothy 1:13–18
description: Hold the pattern of sound teaching and guard the treasure with the Spirit's help; Asia's desertion, and Onesiphorus, who searched Rome until he found the prisoner.
paragraphs: The charge to hold comes in two sentences, and they belong together. “Hold on to the pattern of sound teaching you have heard from me, with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus. Guard the treasure entrusted to you, with the help of the Holy Spirit who dwells in us.” The pattern is something Timothy heard, a shape of teaching with words that give health, held not by clenching but with faith and love. The treasure is something entrusted, and the guarding is not solitary work: the Spirit who dwells in us helps. Jude heard a deposit to guard, the Ephesian elders heard a flock to guard, Timothy in the first letter heard a charge to guard. Here the phrasing is warmest. The treasure is guarded by a man indwelt, not by a man alone.

Then the letter faces the desertion head-on. “You know that everyone in the province of Asia has deserted me, including Phygelus and Hermogenes.” Asia was the province of Ephesus, the ground of Paul's longest ministry and Timothy's own labor, and the report is total in its wording: everyone there has turned away from the prisoner, and two of the deserters are named, men about whom the letter says nothing else. Their names survive only in this sentence, attached to the leaving. Paul does not rail at them. He simply tells his child the state of things, because the next sentence needs the darkness to show what it shows.

Against the desertion stands one household. “May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he has often refreshed me and was unashamed of my chains. Indeed, when he arrived in Rome, he searched diligently until he found me.” In a city where finding a prisoner took effort and standing near one took nerve, Onesiphorus hunted until he found Paul and then kept coming back, refreshing a chained man the way cold water refreshes a tired one. Paul's answer is a prayer with a future in it: “May the Lord grant Onesiphorus His mercy on that day.” And almost as an aside, the letter locates Timothy: “You know very well how much he ministered to me in Ephesus.” Timothy knew this man's service firsthand. The example is not a stranger's. It is a friend both men could picture.

Hold the pattern, guard the treasure, and know that the deserters are not the whole story. One man searched Rome for a prisoner and was not ashamed. The letter now stops looking backward and starts building forward, to the men Timothy himself must raise.

title: Entrust to Faithful Men
subtitle: 2 Timothy 2:1–7
description: Be strong in grace; entrust what you heard to faithful men who will teach others; and the soldier, the competitor, and the hardworking farmer.
paragraphs: Chapter 2 opens with the strengthening word. “You therefore, my child, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.” The strength commanded is not Timothy's temperament improved; it is grace located in Christ, drawn on the way a soldier draws rations. And out of that strength comes the letter's most structural sentence: “And the things that you have heard me say among many witnesses, entrust these to faithful men who will be qualified to teach others as well.” Count the generations in one breath: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and the others those men will teach. The teaching was heard publicly, among many witnesses, nothing whispered in a corner, and its future runs through a chain of entrusted people. Timothy's faithfulness is measured not only by what he keeps but by what he hands on, and to whom: faithful men, qualified to teach.

Then Paul gives his child three pictures of the life, each with its own logic, and each drawn from ordinary work. The soldier: “Join me in suffering, like a good soldier of Christ Jesus. A soldier refrains from entangling himself in civilian affairs, in order to please the one who enlisted him.” The point is focus with a person in view: the soldier stays unentangled not to be severe but to please the one who enlisted him. The competitor: “Likewise, a competitor does not receive the crown unless he competes according to the rules.” The crown exists and is winnable, but not by shortcuts; the rules bind even the gifted. The farmer: “The hardworking farmer should be the first to partake of the crops.” Labor comes before eating, and the laborer's share is right, not stolen. Suffering shared, rules kept, work before reward: three trades, one shape of ministry.

Paul does not explain the pictures to death, and the reason is in the last verse of the passage: “Consider what I am saying, for the Lord will give you insight into all things.” Timothy is treated as a man who can weigh an image and find its bearing himself, with insight promised from the Lord rather than supplied by a commentary. The letter that will shortly call him an unashamed workman gives him work to do right here: consider. From the chain of teachers and the three figures, the telling moves to the center they all serve, Jesus Christ raised from the dead, and the strangest pairing in the letter: a chained man and an unchainable word.

title: The Word of God Cannot Be Chained
subtitle: 2 Timothy 2:8–13
description: Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, descended from David; the chained apostle and the unchained word; endurance for the elect; and the trustworthy saying in four lines.
paragraphs: Before the hardships, the anchor. “Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, descended from David, as proclaimed by my gospel.” The whole faith in one remembrance: a real descendant of David, crucified in the earlier tellings and here summed by the resurrection, raised from the dead. It is for this gospel, Paul says, “for which I suffer to the extent of being chained like a criminal. But the word of God cannot be chained!” The sentence performs what it claims. The apostle's wrists are bound like a common criminal's, and the message he carries moves exactly as freely as it did when he crossed provinces at will. The chain is real. So is its limit. Rome could hold the preacher and could not hold the preaching.

Why endure it, then? The letter answers with the elect in view: “For this reason I endure all things for the sake of the elect, so that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus, with eternal glory.” The suffering is not endured for its own sake or for Paul's reputation. It is aimed at people who will obtain salvation with eternal glory, and that aim makes the chain bearable in the letter's own accounting. God, who guarded Paul's deposit in the earlier passage, is gathering people through Paul's endurance now, and the chained man counts that a fair trade.

Then comes the hymn, introduced the way the letters introduce their settled sayings: “This is a trustworthy saying: If we died with Him, we will also live with Him; if we endure, we will also reign with Him; if we deny Him, He will also deny us; if we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself.” Four lines, two of promise and two of warning, and the telling keeps all four at the weight Paul sets. Dying with him leads to living with him. Enduring leads to reigning. Denying him has an answer, and the answer is his. And the last line holds what the third line threatens inside a greater fact: human faithlessness does not make God faithless, because he cannot act against his own nature. The hymn comforts and warns in the same breath, which is exactly how this letter handles its beloved child, arms around him and eyes open. The next verses turn from the center to the weeds growing around it, and to the workman who must handle the word without shame.

title: A Workman Unashamed
subtitle: 2 Timothy 2:14–19
description: No quarreling over words; the unashamed workman accurately handling the word of truth; talk that spreads like gangrene; and the firm foundation with its two-sided seal.
paragraphs: The chapter turns from endurance to the daily handling of words, and the first command is a reminder with a courtroom edge: “Remind the believers of these things, charging them before God to avoid quarreling over words, which succeeds only in leading the listeners to ruin.” Word quarrels are not treated as harmless sport for sharp minds. Their one success, Paul says with dry precision, is ruining the people listening. Against that stands the verse by which Timothy's whole ministry is measured: “Make every effort to present yourself approved to God, an unashamed workman who accurately handles the word of truth.” The workman image is a craftsman's. A man who cuts the word straight has nothing to be ashamed of when the master inspects the work, and approval from God, not applause from the room, is the standard named.

The opposite trade gets the letter's ugliest picture: “But avoid irreverent, empty chatter, which will only lead to more ungodliness,” and of the men who trade in it, “the talk of such men will spread like gangrene. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have deviated from the truth. They say that the resurrection has already occurred, and they undermine the faith of some.” Gangrene is dead tissue spreading through living flesh, and Paul reaches for it deliberately. The named men, Hymenaeus named in the first letter as well, Philetus only here, were teaching that the resurrection was already past, a claim that quietly empties the faith's future, and some believers' faith was being undermined by it. Empty talk is never only empty. It spreads, it rots, and real people go down with it.

And then, over against the spreading rot, the foundation: “Nevertheless, God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal:” “The Lord knows those who are His,” and, “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord must turn away from iniquity.” The two inscriptions stand side by side the way Paul sets them, God's knowledge of his own on one face, and the human duty to depart from iniquity on the other. Some faith is being undermined; the foundation is not. The church in Ephesus could wobble, teachers could deviate, talk could rot like gangrene, and underneath it all the firm foundation stands with its seal legible. Timothy's workmanship happens on top of something that does not move. The letter goes on to picture that church as a large house full of vessels, some for honor and some for common use, and to ask what kind of vessel Timothy himself will be.

title: Vessels for Honor
subtitle: 2 Timothy 2:20–26
description: The large house and its vessels, cleansing toward honorable use; flee youthful passions and pursue with a pure heart; and the Lord's servant, gentle toward opponents in hope of their escape.
paragraphs: The large house comes first: “A large house contains not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay. Some indeed are for honorable use, but others are for common use.” A great house runs on both kinds, the gold vessel brought out for guests and the clay one put to ordinary work, and Paul does not pretend the church he is describing is all gold. Then the sentence turns toward the reader's own agency: “So if anyone cleanses himself of what is unfit, he will be a vessel for honor: sanctified, useful to the Master, and prepared for every good work.” What a vessel is for is not fixed by its shelf. Cleansing moves a person toward honor, set apart, useful to the Master of the house, ready when a good work needs a tool at hand. The Master in view is the house's owner, and usefulness to him is the promotion the passage offers.

The cleansing takes concrete shape in the next charge: “Flee from youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, together with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart.” Fleeing is only half the motion. The pursuit runs in company, with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart, the same pure heart this letter series keeps aiming at. And the talk wars get their final word: “But reject foolish and ignorant speculation, for you know that it breeds quarreling.” Timothy already knows what such talk produces. He is being reminded, not informed.

Then the passage lands on the servant's manner, and it is the gentlest instruction in a stern letter: “And a servant of the Lord must not be quarrelsome, but must be kind to everyone, able to teach, and forbearing. He must gently reprove those who oppose him, in the hope that God may grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth.” The opponent is not an enemy to crush but a captive to free: “Then they will come to their senses and escape the snare of the devil, who has taken them captive to his will.” A man arguing for the truth treats the person across from him as a prisoner of war behind enemy lines, and reproves him gently because the goal is his escape. Repentance, even here, is God's to grant. The servant's part is kindness with a spine, teaching with forbearance, and hope aimed at the opponent's rescue. The letter then lifts its eyes from the congregation's quarrels to the age itself, and the weather report darkens: in the last days, terrible times will come.

title: In the Last Days
subtitle: 2 Timothy 3:1–9
description: In the last days terrible times: the long list of loves bent inward, a form of godliness denying its power, and Jannes and Jambres, whose advance has a stated limit.
paragraphs: Chapter 3 opens with a command to understand, and what must be understood is a forecast: “But understand this: In the last days terrible times will come.” The times are described by their people: “For men will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, unholy, unloving, unforgiving, slanderous, without self-control, brutal, without love of good, traitorous, reckless, conceited, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God”. The telling keeps the list whole, the way the pattern letters keep their lists whole, because its weight is in its accumulation: love turned inward at every joint, toward self, toward money, toward pleasure, and away from God at the end of the sentence where the contrast lands.

The ugliest line is the religious one: “having a form of godliness but denying its power. Turn away from such as these!” These are not outsiders railing against the faith. They carry its shape, its forms, its vocabulary, and deny the power that makes it real, and Timothy's instruction about them is not debate but distance. Then the passage shows the form at work: “They are the kind who worm their way into households and captivate vulnerable women who are weighed down with sins and led astray by various passions, who are always learning but never able to come to a knowledge of the truth.” The worming image is exact: quiet entry, soft targets, people burdened and restless, fed with endless lessons that never arrive at truth. Always learning, never knowing, is the form of godliness experienced from inside.

Paul closes the passage with two names from Egypt: “Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so also these men oppose the truth. They are depraved in mind and disqualified from the faith.” Exodus tells of Pharaoh's magicians opposing Moses without ever naming them; Jannes and Jambres are the names tradition attached to them, and Paul uses the tradition's names the way Jude reached for tradition about Moses. The comparison carries a limit, and the limit matters as much as the warning: “But they will not advance much further. For just like Jannes and Jambres, their folly will be plain to everyone.” The magicians' contest with Moses ended with their power exposed and their advance stopped. So with these men: opposition is real, damage is real, and the run of it is short. The next passage turns the whole weather report personal, because Timothy has a different history to stand on: he has followed Paul's teaching, conduct, and sufferings up close.

title: Continue in What You Have Learned
subtitle: 2 Timothy 3:10–17
description: You have observed my teaching and my sufferings, and from them all the Lord rescued me; continue in what you have learned; and all Scripture is God-breathed, equipping the man of God completely.
paragraphs: Against the forecast stands a biography. “You, however, have observed my teaching, my conduct, my purpose, my faith, my patience, my love, my perseverance, my persecutions, and the sufferings that came upon me in Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra. What persecutions I endured! Yet the Lord rescued me from all of them.” The list runs from doctrine to scars without a seam: teaching and conduct, faith and patience, and then the named towns where the following cost something. Timothy had been there for Lystra most of all, the town where Paul was stoned and where Timothy's own story with him began, as the Acts telling traced. He does not need the persecutions explained. He watched them. And the verdict on them is deliverance, named plainly: from them all, the Lord rescued me.

The general law follows, at full strength: “Indeed, all who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted, while evil men and imposters go from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived.” Both movements run at once in the letter's world, the godly pressed and the impostors worsening, deceiving others and duped themselves. Timothy's orders inside that world are two words deep: “But as for you, continue in the things you have learned and firmly believed, since you know from whom you have learned them.” Note the anchors: what he learned, and whom he learned it from, the grandmother and mother of the letter's opening standing unnamed behind that whom. And the Scriptures known since childhood are the third anchor: “From infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.”

Then the passage says the thing about those Scriptures that the whole church has carried since: “All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work.” Breathed out by God is the claim, and usefulness is the shape of it: the Scripture teaches, convicts, corrects, and trains, four workings aimed at one result, a man of God complete, lacking no equipment for any good work set before him. Timothy, who has known these writings since he was small enough to be taught them at his grandmother's knee, is not being handed a new book. He is being told what the book he already has is, and what it is for. The letter then rises to its most formal moment: a charge sworn before God himself, to preach this word.

title: Preach the Word
subtitle: 2 Timothy 4:1–5
description: The charge sworn before God and Christ Jesus the judge: preach the word in season and out, reprove, rebuke, encourage; the itching-ears future; and fulfill your ministry.
paragraphs: Chapter 4 opens with the most solemn sentence in the letter, a charge sworn before witnesses no courtroom could hold: “I charge you in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, and in view of His appearing and His kingdom:” Everything Paul is about to command Timothy, he commands with God present, with Christ as coming judge of living and dead, and with the appearing and the kingdom in view. The charge is not advice passed between colleagues. It is testimony laid down before the judge of the world, by a man who expects to stand in that court himself before long, and who writes like it.

Then the charge itself, five commands in one breath: “Preach the word; be prepared in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and encourage with every form of patient instruction.” Preaching is the job whatever the season feels like, convenient or not, welcomed or not. And its three edges are named in order: reprove, rebuke, encourage, the correction and the comfort both carried, both delivered with patience in the teaching rather than heat in the moment. A preacher who only rebukes has dropped a third of the charge; a preacher who only encourages has dropped two thirds of it.

The reason given is a forecast Timothy is meant to work inside, not fear: “For the time will come when men will not tolerate sound doctrine, but with itching ears they will gather around themselves teachers to suit their own desires. So they will turn their ears away from the truth and turn aside to myths.” The itching ears image is exact: hearers shopping for teachers the way restless people scratch an itch, assembling a faculty to say what they already want said. Paul dates none of it and names no one in it. It is the stated future his child will preach into, and the letter leaves its calendar where Paul left it, with him.

Against that future stands one man's job description, in four phrases: “But you, be sober in all things, endure hardship, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry.” Sober when the room is drunk on novelty. Enduring when the work costs. Doing an evangelist's work, carrying the good news outward and not only tending the convinced. And fulfilling the ministry, finishing the whole assignment rather than its comfortable parts. The charge sworn before God lands there, in a man's daily posture. What gives it its weight is what Paul says next about himself, and the next words are the ones this whole letter has been walking toward: I am already being poured out.

title: I Have Kept the Faith
subtitle: 2 Timothy 4:6–8
description: Already being poured out like a drink offering, the race finished and the faith kept, and the crown of righteousness laid up, for Paul and for all who crave his appearing.
paragraphs: Here the letter says what it has been circling since its first chapter. “For I am already being poured out like a drink offering, and the time of my departure is at hand.” A drink offering was wine poured out entirely at the altar, nothing held back, nothing recoverable, and Paul treats his own life as already mid-pour. Departure is his chosen word, a traveler and soldier's word, the striking of a tent and the loosing of a ship, and he states its timing without drama: the time is at hand. This is not a man surprised by his chains. It is a man reading them correctly.

The three sentences that follow are the most famous self-assessment in the New Testament, and they are kept whole: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.” Fight, race, trust: the soldier's contest, the runner's course, the guarded deposit of the whole letter series held to the end. Every verb is finished tense. Paul is not resolving to do these things; he is reporting that they are done. The man who told Timothy the competitor is crowned only if he competes according to the rules now reports his own race as run out to its line, and the faith he charged his child to guard, he has kept.

And the crown is already in view: “From now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to me on that day” and then, because the BSB breaks the sentence with a dash, the promise widens in its own fragment: “and not only to me, but to all who crave His appearing.” The judge who awards it is righteous, the opposite of the empty courts Paul has been standing in, and the day of the award is the same that day this letter has pointed to since its first chapter, when God guards deposits and grants mercy. Paul does not hoard the crown at the end. The man who began the chapter charging Timothy before the judge of living and dead ends his self-assessment by opening the promise to everyone who craves the appearing, his beloved child first among them. What remains is only the practical end of a real letter: who has gone, who is left, what to bring, and how soon to come.

title: Come Before Winter
subtitle: 2 Timothy 4:9–22
description: Come quickly; Demas gone and only Luke remaining; bring Mark, the cloak, and the parchments; Alexander warned against; the Lord stood by me at my first defense; and come before winter.
paragraphs: The last stretch of the letter is a roll call, and it begins with urgency: “Make every effort to come to me quickly, because Demas, in his love of this world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica. Crescens has gone to Galatia, and Titus to Dalmatia. Only Luke is with me.” Demas, once listed among Paul's fellow workers in the earlier letters, is recorded here with his reason attached, love of this world, and the desertion answers the Asia desertion of the first chapter at the personal range. Others are simply gone on assignment. One man remains, and the telling lets the sentence land: only Luke is with me. The beloved physician of the Colossians letter is the last companion named at Paul's side.

Into that emptiness come the requests, and the first of them is a small resurrection of an old story: “Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is useful to me in the ministry.” Mark, who deserted the first journey and split Paul and Barnabas over his worth years ago, as the Acts telling traced, is now summoned by name and pronounced useful by the man who once refused to take him. The letter does not comment on the repair. It simply makes the request, and lets the request be the comment. Then the errands: “Tychicus, however, I have sent to Ephesus. When you come, bring the cloak that I left with Carpus at Troas, and my scrolls, especially the parchments.” A cloak against the cold of a prison winter, scrolls, above all the parchments: at the end of everything this letter carries, the apostle asks for his coat and his books, and any reader who has wondered whether faith makes a man less human has the letter's own answer.

One name carries a warning: “Alexander the coppersmith did great harm to me. The Lord will repay him according to his deeds. You too should beware of him, for he has vigorously opposed our message.” Paul names an Alexander in the first letter to Timothy as well; whether they are the same man, this letter does not say, and the telling does not settle it. What is settled is the posture: repayment belongs to the Lord, and Timothy's part is watchfulness, not revenge.

Then the courtroom memory: “At my first defense, no one stood with me, but everyone deserted me. May it not be charged against them. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the message would be fully proclaimed, and all the Gentiles would hear it. So I was delivered from the mouth of the lion.” The empty defense and the full proclamation stand in one paragraph. Everyone left, the Lord stood, and the message got preached to the Gentiles through the abandoned man. The confidence closes over the whole life, past and future: “And the Lord will rescue me from every evil action and bring me safely into His heavenly kingdom. To Him be the glory forever and ever. Amen.”

And then, greetings, because even a last letter ends like a letter: “Greet Prisca and Aquila, as well as the household of Onesiphorus. Erastus has remained at Corinth, and Trophimus I left sick in Miletus. Make every effort to come to me before winter. Eubulus sends you greetings, as do Pudens, Linus, Claudia, and all the brothers.” Before winter, when the sea travel closed and the cold came into the cell: the most human deadline in the New Testament. The final two sentences divide their gifts with care: “The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you all.” Singular for the spirit of the beloved child, plural for the whole church that would hear the letter read. Grace be with you all is where the pastoral letters end their speaking, and the next book in this series is the shortest of them, a charge about appointing elders on an island, Titus.
